Thessaloniki New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Stavroupoli, Greece

Not demolished. Thessaloniki, which grew into the largest and most famous Jewish community in Greece, first recorded Jewish settlement around 140 BCE; a Byzantine-era community of 500 grew as Romaniot Jews were exiled to Istanbul at the start of Ottoman rule (1453), replaced by waves of Spanish and Portuguese immigration forming distinct Sephardi congregations under a unifying umbrella community. Population reached 13,225 (of 24,315 total) by 1520-25; Rabbi Moshe Almosnino achieved the community's autonomy from Turkish authority in 1567, and the city became renowned for redeeming captives and, later, for the messianic Shabbetai Zvi movement. Population fell from 30,000 (1714-15) to 23,000 by 1788 amid epidemics and fires, though the community continued growing - 36 synagogues and a large school system by 1828, with the Alliance Israelite Universelle expanding vocational education from 1873. Population reached 40,000-50,000 by 1876-80; a Jewish hospital opened in 1903, and by 1910 some 60 religious study institutes operated. A secret 1908 Zionist organization was Greece's first; a devastating 1917 fire destroyed 34 of 37 synagogues and hundreds of Jewish institutions. Between the World Wars, an extensive Sephardi institutional network persisted, with 40 active synagogues on the eve of WWII. A total of 48,533 Jews were deported to death camps - by war's end, Thessaloniki's status as the great center of European Sephardic Jewry had been effectively destroyed. About 400 survivors returned postwar, reestablishing Greece's second-largest Jewish community after Athens. This cemetery's founding is unknown, presumed 18th-19th century.
